sections.text: Iʿrab of the Dual
The dual (muthanna) is a noun denoting two (m.) or two (f.), formed by adding an alif and nun, or a yaʾ and nun, to its singular; and it is valid to strip this addition and conjoin its like to it.

items: muʿallima-tun, muʿallimatan-i (a teacher f., two teachers f.)

sections.text: This lesson is devoted to the iʿrab of the dual: its signs, its positions in the sentence, what is annexed to it (mulhaq), what merely resembles it without being it, and the changes that affect a word's structure when it is made dual. The definition of the dual and the mechanics of forming it were detailed earlier in the lesson 'The Singular, the Dual, and the Plural'.
First: The Signs of Iʿrab of the Dual
The dual is inflected with letters, not with short vowels: nominative with the alif (instead of damma), and accusative and genitive with the yaʾ (instead of fatha and kasra).

items.text: — The two engineers attended. (nominative with alif)
— The manager rewarded the two engineers. (accusative with yaʾ)
— People praised the two engineers. (genitive with yaʾ)

rows: Subject, nominative, its sign the alif
Direct object, accusative, its sign the yaʾ
Genitive noun, its sign the yaʾ

sections.text: The nun of the dual always carries a kasra in all three cases, and it stands in place of the tanwin of the singular noun; this is why it drops upon annexation (idafa), just as tanwin drops.

items.text: — The two books are beneficial. (the nun takes kasra in the nominative)
— I borrowed the two books. (the nun takes kasra in the accusative)

sections.text: Why does the nun of the dual carry a kasra while the nun of the sound masculine plural carries a fatha?

Because the dual and the sound masculine plural share the yaʾ as the sign of the accusative and genitive; had the nun been identical in both, one would be confused with the other. So the Arabs distinguished them in two ways: a kasra on the nun of the dual and a fatha on the nun of the plural, and a fatha before the yaʾ of the dual and a kasra before the yaʾ of the plural. Thus you say 'karramtu al-talibayni' for two, and 'karramtu al-talibina' for a group.
Second: The Dual in the Positions of Iʿrab

The dual is a declinable noun that occupies every position a singular noun occupies; its position never changes, only its sign does — the alif in place of damma, and the yaʾ in place of fatha and kasra.
1 — The Dual in a Nominative Position

items.text: — The two students are diligent. (subject and predicate, nominative with alif)
— The two players won. (subject of the verb, nominative with alif)
— The two top students were rewarded. (deputy subject, nominative with alif)
— The two friends were cooperative. (noun of kana, nominative with alif)

sections.text: 2 — The Dual in an Accusative Position

items.text: — I read two books. (direct object, accusative with yaʾ)
— Indeed the two students are diligent. (noun of inna, accusative with yaʾ)
— The two boys became energetic. (predicate of asbaha, accusative with yaʾ)
— The two men came forward hurrying. (circumstantial accusative, with yaʾ)
— The two brothers travelled for two days. (adverbial object, accusative with yaʾ)

sections.text: 3 — The Dual in a Genitive Position

items.text: — I greeted the two guests. (genitive after a preposition, its sign the yaʾ)
— This is the two students' book. (second term of annexation, genitive with yaʾ)
— I passed by two generous men. (adjective, genitive with yaʾ)

sections.text: If the dual occurs as a vocative and is a proper name or an intended indefinite, it is built (mabni) on what it would be raised with — the alif — in the place of the accusative of the vocative; so do not call it 'accusative with the yaʾ'.

items.text: — O two students, strive! (vocative built on the alif, in the place of the accusative)
— O two Muhammads, come! (vocative built on the alif, in the place of the accusative)

sections.text: Third: Dropping the Nun upon Annexation

The nun of the dual drops when it is annexed, because it stands in place of tanwin, and tanwin drops upon annexation. Thus 'taliba al-ʿilm' is originally 'al-talibani', and 'kitabay al-tilmidh' is originally 'al-kitabani'.

items.text: — The two students of knowledge attended. (subject, nominative with alif; the nun dropped for annexation)
— I read the pupil's two books. (direct object, accusative with yaʾ; the nun dropped for annexation)
— I looked into the student's two notebooks. (genitive with yaʾ; the nun dropped for annexation)

sections.text: Dropping the nun for annexation does not change the sign of iʿrab: an annexed dual stays nominative with the alif and accusative and genitive with the yaʾ — only the nun is gone.
The Dual Annexed to the Speaker's Yaʾ

When the dual is annexed to the speaker's yaʾ, its nun drops; its alif remains in the nominative ('sadiqaya'), and its yaʾ is assimilated into the speaker's yaʾ in the accusative and genitive ('sadiqayya').

items.text: — My two friends attended. (subject, nominative with alif)
— I visited my two friends. (direct object, accusative with yaʾ)
— I greeted my two friends. (genitive with yaʾ)

sections.text: Fourth: What Is Annexed to the Dual (al-Mulhaq bi-l-Muthanna)

What is annexed to the dual: words inflected exactly like the dual — alif in the nominative, yaʾ in the accusative and genitive — without being a true dual, because the condition of stripping-and-conjoining is not met in them, or because they have no singular from their own root.

items: ithnani and ithnatani: they have no singular from their own root — Arabic has no 'ithnun' or 'ithnatun'.
thintani: a variant of 'ithnatani', with the same ruling.
kila and kilta: when annexed to a pronoun, because their form is singular while their meaning is dual.
ithna ʿashara and ithnata ʿashrata: their first part is inflected like the dual, while their second part is built on the fatha.

items.text: — Two of the students passed. (subject, nominative with alif, being annexed to the dual)
— I honored two of the female winners. (direct object, accusative with yaʾ)
— Twelve students attended. (subject, nominative with alif; the second part built on the fatha)

sections.text: Kila and Kilta

If 'kila' and 'kilta' are annexed to a pronoun, they are inflected like the dual: alif in the nominative and yaʾ in the accusative and genitive. If they are annexed to an overt noun, they are inflected with estimated (muqaddara) vowels on the alif, like a shortened (maqsur) noun.

items.text: — Both of the two men came. (emphasis, nominative with alif, being annexed to a pronoun)
— I honored both of the two students. (emphasis, accusative with yaʾ)
— I greeted both of the two girls. (emphasis, genitive with yaʾ)
— Both of the two men are generous. (subject, nominative with an estimated damma on the alif)
— I saw both of the two men. (direct object, accusative with an estimated fatha on the alif)
— I greeted both of the two girls. (genitive with an estimated kasra on the alif)

rows: Inflected like the dual, with alif and yaʾ
Nominative with an estimated damma on the alif
Accusative with an estimated fatha on the alif

sections.text: 'Kila' and 'kilta' take a singular predicate, in deference to their form: 'kila al-rajulayni karimun', 'kilta al-fatatayni muʾaddabatun'. The sense may occasionally be deferred to instead, giving a dual predicate, but that is rare.
Fifth: What Resembles the Dual but Is Not of It

Not everything ending in an alif-and-nun or a yaʾ-and-nun is a dual; the alif and nun may be augments in a singular noun — e.g. ʿUthman, Salman, ghadban (angry), ʿatshan (thirsty). These are singular nouns, inflected with short vowels, not with letters.

items.text: — ʿUthman attended. (subject, nominative with damma, since it is singular, not dual)
— I saw an angry man. (adjective, accusative with fatha, since it is singular, not dual)

sections.text: The test: a dual can be stripped of its alif and nun with its like conjoined to it — 'talibani' means 'a student and a student' — whereas 'ʿUthman' admits no such thing.
Is there any other visible mark by which we may tell the dual from such a singular?

Yes, two visible marks. First, the nun of the dual always carries a kasra, whereas the nun of a word like 'ʿUthmanu' follows the word's own iʿrab, taking damma, fatha, or kasra. Second, the nun of the dual drops upon annexation — you say 'taliba al-ʿilmi' — while the nun of 'ʿUthman' never drops; one never says 'ʿUthma al-qawmi'.
Sixth: Making the Maqsur, Manqus, and Mamdud Dual
The shortened noun (maqsur) when made dual: its alif is returned to its origin (waw or yaʾ) if it is the third letter, and turned into a yaʾ if it is the fourth letter or beyond.
The defective noun (manqus) when made dual: its elided yaʾ is restored and the dual is built upon it.

The extended noun (mamdud) when made dual: if its hamza is original it stays as it is; if it is the hamza of the feminine it turns into a waw; and if it is converted from an original letter or augmented for quadriliteralization, both forms are permitted.

items: kisaʾun, kisaʾani — kisawani (a garment, two garments)

rows: The alif returns to its origin
The alif turns into a yaʾ
The hamza turns into a waw

sections.text: These changes occur in the structure of the word, not in its iʿrab: a dual formed from them is nominative with the alif and accusative and genitive with the yaʾ, like every other dual.

items.text: — The two youths came. (subject, nominative with alif)
— I asked the two judges. (direct object, accusative with yaʾ)
— We travelled in the two deserts. (genitive with yaʾ)

sections.text: Do not confuse the yaʾ of the dual with the yaʾ of the sound masculine plural in the accusative and genitive. The difference: the letter before the dual's yaʾ carries a fatha and its nun a kasra, while the letter before the plural's yaʾ carries a kasra and its nun a fatha.

items.text: — I honored the two students. (dual: accusative with yaʾ, preceded by a fatha)
— I honored the students. (sound masculine plural: accusative with yaʾ, preceded by a kasra)

sections.text: Model Iʿrab (1)

items.text: — The two diligent students won two prizes.

sections.text: faza: a past-tense verb, built on the fatha. al-talibani: the subject of the verb, nominative, its sign the alif because it is a dual, the nun standing in place of the tanwin of a singular noun. al-mujtahidani: an adjective qualifying 'al-talibani', nominative, its sign the alif because it is a dual. bi-jaʾizatayni: 'bi' is a preposition, and 'jaʾizatayni' a genitive noun, its sign the yaʾ because it is a dual. The verbal clause is an opening clause with no place in iʿrab.
Model Iʿrab (2)

items.text: — Indeed both of the two girls are well-mannered.

sections.text: inna: an abrogating particle built on the fatha, conveying emphasis. kilta: the noun of inna, accusative, its sign an estimated fatha on the alif, prevented from appearing by impossibility, because it is annexed to an overt noun; and it is the first term of annexation. al-fatatayni: the second term of annexation, genitive, its sign the yaʾ because it is a dual. muʾaddabatun: the predicate of inna, nominative, its sign the visible damma; the predicate was made singular in deference to the form of 'kilta'.
From the Noble Qurʾan
Allah Most High said: "Said two men from among those who feared" — Quran 5:23 (Sahih International)
'Rajulani' is the subject of the verb, nominative, its sign the alif because it is a dual, its nun carrying a kasra in place of the tanwin.
And Allah Most High said: "But for he who has feared the position of his Lord are two gardens" — Quran 55:46 (Sahih International)
'Jannatani' is a delayed subject, nominative, its sign the alif because it is a dual; the prepositional phrase 'li-man' stands in the place of the nominative as a fronted predicate.
And Allah Most High said: "Each of the two gardens produced its fruit" — Quran 18:33 (Sahih International)

'Kilta' is the subject, nominative, its sign an estimated damma on the alif, because it is annexed to an overt noun; and it is the first term of annexation. 'Al-jannatayni' is the second term of annexation, genitive, its sign the yaʾ because it is a dual. The clause 'atat ukulaha' stands in the place of the nominative as the predicate, and the verb was made singular in deference to the form of 'kilta'.
And Allah Most High said: "Whether one or both of them reach old age with you" — Quran 17:23 (Sahih International)

'Kilahuma' is conjoined to 'ahaduhuma', nominative, its sign the alif because it is annexed to the dual; it took this inflection precisely because it is annexed to a pronoun, and it is the first term of annexation, while 'huma' is an attached pronoun built in the place of the genitive as the second term of annexation.
